title: What an address is made of

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. run.js starts the cupboard server, runs your functions against it and prints every request and answer.

tasks.title: Take an address apart
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/address.js`, make `addressParts(address)` take a whole address as text and give back an object with four properties:

- `scheme`: the word at the start, without its colon, like `'https'`
- `host`: the name of the computer only, like `'listen.heronsgate.example'`
- `port`: a number. When the address writes no port, it is the port its scheme uses when none is written
- `path`: the part after the host, starting with its slash, like `'/shows/dawn-chorus'`

Check calls `addressParts` with addresses of its own, with and without a port, and compares each of the four parts.
nextSteps: Make a `URL` from the address, as the lesson shows, and print it to see its properties.
Pick out the scheme, the host and the path, and look at what each one holds exactly.
Turn the port into a number, and decide what it is when the address writes none.
Run `node run.js` and compare both Task 1 lines with the addresses they read.
hints: `new URL(address)` takes the address apart for you. Print it with `console.log` and look at `protocol`, `hostname`, `host`, `port` and `pathname`.
Some properties hold a little more or less than the task asks for: `protocol` keeps the colon, `host` keeps the port, and `port` is text that is empty when the address writes no port.

Start with `const url = new URL(address)`. The scheme is `url.protocol` without its last character, and when `url.port` is `''` the port is `443` for https and `80` for http; otherwise it is `Number(url.port)`.

tasks.title: Put an address together
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `pageAddress(base, path)` give back the whole address of one page as text. `base` is the address of a server, like `'http://localhost:5133'`, and it may or may not end with a slash. `path` starts with a slash, like `'/shows'`. The address must have exactly one slash between the host and the path.

Check calls `pageAddress` with bases of its own, some ending in a slash and some not.
nextSteps: Try joining the two texts with `+` and run `node run.js`.
Now call it yourself with a base that ends in a slash and look at the slashes.
Let `URL` put the two together instead, as the lesson shows.
Give back the address as text, not the `URL` object.
hints: Joining two texts with `+` keeps every character of both, so a slash at the end of one and a slash at the start of the other become two.
`new URL` can take a second value: the address to start from. Then the first value can be a path, and URL works out where the slashes go.
`new URL(path, base)` gives a URL object, and its `href` property is the whole address as text.

tasks.title: Ask for a page and read it
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `fetchText(address)` send a request for the page at `address` with `fetch`, wait for the answer, and give back the text of the answer's body.

Check starts a server of its own with pages of its own, calls `fetchText` with their addresses, and looks at both sides: the request its server received, and the text `fetchText` gave back.
nextSteps: Send the request with `fetch(address)` and wait for the answer with `await`.
Print the answer to see what you got: it is not the text yet.
Read the body as text, wait for that too, and give it back.
Run `node run.js`: the request and the answer for Task 3 are printed under it.
hints: `fetch` gives back a promise of the answer, not the answer. `await` waits for it, and only works inside a function marked `async`, which this one already is.
The answer is an object with the status, the headers and a way to read the body. Reading the body takes a moment too, so it also gives a promise.
Two lines: `const response = await fetch(address)`, then `return await response.text()`.
